extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in computational number theory, lattice algorithms, and cryptanalysis (people implementing/analyzing lattice enumeration and BDD/CVP solvers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and implementing pruned lattice-point enumeration (Schnorr–Euchner style DFS with cylinder pruning) to solve bounded-distance decoding / closest-vector problems on (possibly unbalanced) integer lattices; choosing pruning functions, lattice construction parameters, and algorithmic bounds to trade off cost vs coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension vs practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: To maximize (2.6) or (2.7) it makes sense to take N as large as possible, but high-quality lattice reduction becomes extremely time-consuming for N ≥ 100; non-trivial lattice tasks (e.g., closest lattice point) typically run in time exponential in N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the desire to include many summands (large N) with the exponential growth of lattice-reduction/enumeration cost. Treat N ≥ 100 as impractical for the trial-and-error strategy used in [KR23].

rubrics_metrics.name: When to prefer enumeration over reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the lattice dimension is moderate, it is possible to enumerate all lattice points within any small ball, or many points inside a larger ball; enumeration is naturally a DFS of a carefully constructed tree (Schnorr–Euchner enumeration, adapted by GNR10 and LN13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use enumeration when dimension is moderate and the target region is small enough that enumeration (possibly pruned) is computationally feasible; prefer DFS enumeration trees for zero-centered or shifted balls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running-time dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: The running time of enumeration depends on the radius R and the basis B, but is typically super-exponential in n, even if L ∩ S is small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect worst-case super-exponential behaviour; use pruning and good bases to reduce practical cost. Estimate performance as a function of R and Gram–Schmidt properties of B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pruned enumeration & pruning set P
rubrics_metrics.description: Pruned enumeration uses a pruning set P ⊆ ℝ^n and outputs L ∩ (t + P); for suitable P enumerating L ∩ (t + P) is much cheaper than L ∩ S, yet under mild heuristics is expected to cover most of L ∩ S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design P to trade coverage vs cost: smaller P reduces enumerated nodes but risks missing solutions. Treat the pruning set as a random variable depending on basis B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cylinder pruning definition (P_f(B,R))
rubrics_metrics.description: In GNR10, the pruning set P is defined by a function f:{1,…,n}→[0,1], a radius R>0 and basis B as P_f(B,R) = { x ∈ ℝ^n s.t. ||π_{n+1-i}(x)|| ≤ f(i) R for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n } (intersection of cylinders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cylinder pruning: choose f(i) in [0,1] to set coordinate-wise projection bounds. This representation makes pruning geometrically interpretable and amenable to volume estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: GNR decision algorithm guarantee
rubrics_metrics.description: GNR10 provides an algorithm which, given (B, R, f), decides if L ∩ P_f(B,R) is non-empty, and if so outputs one element of L ∩ P_f(B,R). It can be modified to handle L ∩ (t + P_f(B,R)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When implementing, ensure the algorithm returns an element if one exists; extend to shifted targets t by the LN13 modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing f from projection statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: If x denotes the projection of a random unit vector onto an i-dimensional subspace then ||x||^2 ∼ Beta(i/2,(n−i)/2). In experiments the authors used f^2(i) = μ_i + 2 σ_i (expectation plus twice std. dev.) — a function close to linear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose f by modeling projection norms with Beta distributions; the rule f^2(i)=μ_i+2σ_i is a practical heuristic intended to make P_f cover most of the projected mass. Use this to pick pruning profiles close to linear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate cost and coverage via volume and Gaussian heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: GNR10 computed tight lower/upper bounds for vol(P_f(B,R)) and estimated the cost of enumerating L∩S∩P_f using the Gaussian heuristic |L∩S| ≈ vol S / det L (applied to projected lattices); these estimates are usually accurate and applicable in CVP case as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use volume bounds and the Gaussian heuristic to predict enumeration cost and expected number of lattice points. Apply these estimates to tune R, f, and basis choices before running heavy enumerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: View pruning set as basis-dependent random variable
rubrics_metrics.description: The pruning set P should be viewed as a random variable: it depends on the choice of basis B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different reduced bases yield different effective pruning behaviour; when evaluating pruning performance, consider basis variability and possibly average heuristics over typical bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm 1 inputs and required data
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithm 1 requires: a reduced basis B=(b1,…,bm), a target vector t = ∑_{i=1}^m t_i b_i, bounding radii R_1^2 ≤ … ≤ R_m^2, Gram–Schmidt matrix μ = (⟨b_i,b_j^*⟩/||b_j^*||^2), and the squared norms ||b_j^*||^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure basis is reduced and compute Gram–Schmidt data accurately. Provide non-decreasing R_i^2 as per the algorithm preconditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Node acceptance and duplicate-avoidance invariant
rubrics_metrics.description: The algorithm enumerates vectors v ∈ L whose projections satisfy ||π_{m+1-k}(v−t)|| ≤ R_k for all k, and enforces the extra constraint that there is no x_1 ∈ ℤ with ||v + x_1 b_1 − t|| < ||v − t|| to avoid returning too many vectors when b_1 is much shorter than det(L)^{1/m}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement the duplicate-avoidance check to prevent returning trivial translations along very short basis vectors. Maintain the projection bounds invariants to prune the DFS correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational node test and return condition
rubrics_metrics.description: During the DFS maintain ρ_k (squared norm contribution) and accept the current node if ρ_k ≤ R_{m+1-k}^2; if k=1 return (v_1,…,v_m) as solution; if k reaches m+1 return ∅ (no solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement rho accumulation and compare with the appropriate R bound for pruning. Follow the k increment/decrement rules to traverse the enumeration tree and detect success/failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lattice construction for optimizing h_P or h_StR (matrix (3.2))
rubrics_metrics.description: For each nontrivial zero ρ with Im ρ > 0 define α^* (attenuated α depending on γ), corresponding γ and ψ, choose parameters ν, ν_y, ν_t and consider the integer lattice L spanned by rows of the (N+1)×(N+1) matrix (3.2) whose first row entries are ⌊√(α_i^*) γ_i 2^{ν_y}⌋ and diagonal-like entries ⌊√(α_i^*) 2π 2^{ν}⌋, and last column includes 2^{ν_t}; the target vector t has components ⌊√(α_i^*) ψ_i 2^{ν}⌋ and a trailing 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building lattices to search for large values of h_P or h_StR follow the scaling and floor conventions in (3.2). Choose α^* differently depending on whether optimizing h_P (use exp(-1.5e-6 γ^2)) or h_StR (use exp(-3e-9 γ^2)). Set ν, ν_y, ν_t to control balance/unbalance of the lattice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace α by α^* when optimizing h_P/h_StR
rubrics_metrics.description: Use α^* = α exp(−1.5·10^{−6} γ^2) to find large |h_P|, or α^* = α exp(−3·10^{−9} γ^2) to find large |h_StR|; α^* replaces α from (2.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the attenuated α^* to bias the lattice construction towards optimizing the quantity of interest (h_P or h_StR) instead of q_N as in prior work [OtR85].

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter K and success criterion (expected inequality)
rubrics_metrics.description: For γ ≥ 1 define K := γ sqrt((N+1)/(2π e)) det(L)^{1/(N+1)} (K is an approximate radius). The search aims to find u ∈ L with ||u − t|| < K, which (after algebra) translates to inequalities like (3.4) and (3.5) bounding modular differences and a weighted sum ∑ α_i^* |γ_i^* y − ψ_i^*|_{2π}^2 < K^2 / 2^{2ν}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use K to set radius thresholds and predict success probability. Translate the geometric condition into arithmetic inequalities on x,y and tune ν and other scaling exponents so the expected inequality is achievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose unbalanced lattices via ν ≫ ν_y
rubrics_metrics.description: The lattice defined by (3.2) is unbalanced when ν ≫ ν_y: then the i-th coefficient of the first row is much smaller than the i-th diagonal coefficient, so the first row has norm much smaller than det(L)^{1/(N+1)} and is likely to be a shortest vector of L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the lattice appears unbalanced and the first row becomes shortest (undesired trivial short vector), adjust ν and ν_y to rebalance. Use this diagnosis to avoid pathological short vectors that make enumeration trivial or misleading.
